extracted.intended_audience: students and coaches preparing for math olympiads / advanced problem solvers in trigonometry
extracted.subtask_description: Solving and writing rigorous solutions to advanced trigonometry contest problems using substitutions, standard identities, known inequalities, geometric reasoning, and polynomial/analytic techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trig-to-algebra substitution (cot/tan substitutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce algebraic variables for trig ratios (e.g., "Let cot A = x, cot B = y, and cot C = z") so that trig relations become algebraic ones (for triangles, use identities like xy + yz + zx = 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 19 sets cot A = x etc., uses xy + yz + zx = 1 to reduce the desired inequality to a homogeneous algebraic inequality. Use these substitutions to convert trig inequalities into symmetric polynomial inequalities that are easier to manipulate. Ensure domain assumptions (angles in (0, π)) are respected when substituting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce to and apply classical algebraic inequalities (Schur, AM-GM, Cauchy, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: After algebraic reduction, identify standard inequalities that apply (e.g., show expression is equivalent to Schur's inequality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 19 reduces x^3 + y^3 + z^3 + 6xyz ≥ (x+y+z)(xy+yz+zx) to x(x−y)(x−z) + ... ≥ 0 and cites Schur. Pattern: reduce to known inequality, then invoke it. Check homogeneity to allow normalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use angle representations for iterative maps (sin^2 doubling representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent sequence terms as sin^2 of an angle so iterations correspond to angle-doubling: if a_{n+1} = 4 a_n(1−a_n) and a1 = sin^2 θ then a_k = sin^2(2^{k−1} θ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 20 shows a_n = sin^2 2^{n−1} θ and counts t giving a_{1998}=0 by solving sin(2^{1997} θ)=0. Use this technique to convert logistic-type recurrences into angle iteration; mind domain (0≤t≤1) and count distinct k modulo the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use law of sines / Ceva and product-to-sum / sum-to-product identities in angle-chasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the law of sines or Ceva's theorem together with product-to-sum or sum-to-product trig identities to relate interior angle measures and deduce specific angle values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 21 uses Ceva/law of sines and product-to-sum to derive an equation in x and conclude x=20°, proving the triangle is isosceles. Method: translate directed angle conditions to sine ratios, then simplify with product-to-sum formulas; consider monotonicity of sine on (0,90°).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial / Chebyshev approach for functional/compositional problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify or construct polynomials (often Chebyshev polynomials) to exploit composition properties (e.g., P_m(P_n(x)) = P_n(P_m(x))). Use polynomial coefficient comparison and known values T_n(cos θ) = cos nθ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 24 proves uniqueness of a sequence P_k with P_i ∘ P_j commuting with P_2 by comparing coefficients and showing P_n(x)=2T_n(x/2). Use identity on interval (e.g., [−2,2]) and extend by polynomial equality. Compare leading coefficients and equate coefficients successively where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express geometric quantities via R, r and trig functions to decide signs/equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Write lengths and expressions in terms of circumradius R, inradius r, and trig functions; factor trig terms (e.g., factor cos 2z) to determine sign (positive/zero/negative) depending on angle types (acute/right/obtuse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 25 expresses s = a + b − 2R − 2r as 2R·(expression) and factors cos 2z to show sign depends on angle C being acute, right, or obtuse. Use extended law of sines and Euler relation |OI|^2 = R(R−2r) where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use projections and cosine to lower-bound lengths and sum inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Project segments perpendicularly to a base and compare segment lengths with their projections to obtain lower bounds and sum inequalities for polygonal chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 26 bounds |EF|, |DE|, |FD| via projections E1, F1 and cosines of angles, then sums to obtain ≥ 1/2 perimeter, with equality characterization for the equilateral case. Technique: relate actual length ≥ projected length; add cyclic inequalities and use known trig-sum bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometric substitution + identity manipulation and case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Make substitutions like tan x = a or set sin/cos variables, rewrite inequalities using sum-to-product, double-angle, or product-to-sum formulas, then analyze by monotonicity or separate cases for parameter ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 27 converts the inequality into cos-based form using tan-substitution and proves for two cases (0<a,b≤1 and ab≥3) using double-angle and product-to-sum formulas plus monotonicity of sine/cosine on specified ranges. Always track ranges (e.g., x,y in (0,90°), signs of cos(x−y)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescoping / recurrence manipulation using tangent addition and triple-angle formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Express terms as tan(α+β) or similar to produce relations among tk and tk+1 that telescope when multiplied, often using addition/subtraction formulas and triple-angle recurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 23 defines tk = tan((3k−1)π/(3n−1)) and shows tk+1/tk = (3−t_k^2)/(1−3t_k^2) via triple-angle formula; product telescopes to prove product uk vk = 1. Good for products/ratios over arithmetic sequences of angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Chebyshev / interpolation bounds to relate products of differences and leading coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Lagrange interpolation to Chebyshev polynomials and equate leading coefficients to obtain sum/product inequalities involving nodes x_i in [−1,1].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 33 uses interpolation of T_{n−1} at points x1,...,xn and |T_{n−1}(x_k)| ≤ 1 to deduce 2^{n−2} ≤ ∑ 1/t_k, where t_k are products of |x_j − x_i|. Method applies when bounding extremal polynomials or Vandermonde-like products on [−1,1].

rubrics_metrics.name: Use power-mean, Cauchy–Schwarz and AM-GM inequalities in trig-sum contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply classical inequalities (power mean, Cauchy–Schwarz, AM-GM) to sums of sines/cosines or combinations like ∑ sin^2 xi = 1 to deduce inequalities between linear and quadratic sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Problem 34 uses power-mean to show 3∑ sin xi ≤ ∑ cos xi given ∑ sin^2 xi =1. Problems 35, 36, 38 use Cauchy/AM-GM with trigonometric substitutions. Typical pattern: convert to sums of squares or products, then apply inequality; pay attention to normalization and equality conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize equality cases by forcing squared differences to zero
rubrics_metrics.description: After completing squares or producing nonnegative squared terms, identify equality by solving the vanishing condition (e.g., y sin nC − z sin nB = 0 or proportionality relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In Problem 42(b) the inequality reduces to (y sin nC − z sin nB)^2 ≥ 0; equality holds iff y sin nC = z sin nB. Use such conditions to fully characterize when equality occurs and relate them back to original variables (angles or side-length ratios).
